blocks.x: You can give your name first.
Maude Bakke Johnson.
Ready? That's good. It's running. When were you born?
I was born in 1908, August the 24th.
Where was?
In New Iberia.
In New Iberia.
In Louisiana, uh-huh.
Can you tell a thing about your family? Your family name was Bakke?
Yeah, my family name was Bakke. John Bakke was my father. How did they spell that name? B-A-L-Q-U-E. Q-U-E. Oh, yeah. No T on the end. No. That's the way he spelled his name.
Do you know how he was related to the Bakke's that George Bakke, the clarinetist here? I know Bunk said you were a cousin of his, he told me once.

I think that was my daddy's nephew, uh, nephew's son. And they lived in New Orleans, but they all came from Appalucie. They all came from the other- That was his home in Appalucie. The other Bakke's didn't seem to be clearing out of the ground. Yeah.
Um, are there still some of them living out there in their family?
Well, I had a sister on my daddy's side, but I don't know if she's still living, but all my dads, my other brothers are dead. They're all dead.
Oh, yeah.
The last one was living in, uh, Beaumont, and he was the last one died.
Well, uh, I think we might ask about your sister that's living in New Iberia. Her name is, uh- George Bakke Dixon.
Dixon.
Yeah. And is Mr. Dixon still living?
Yeah, he's still living. How is he now?
I haven't heard Linda.
He's doing pretty good now.
Um, but he- He's one they call Candy, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah. Is he able to talk? I wondered maybe if we could interview him someday. Yeah, he could talk. Because he knew quite a bit about Bunk, too.
Yeah, because through him, that's the way I met Bunk. Oh, is that right?
Yeah. That's what I'd like to know, if you can tell about that while we're talking.

Well, I was- we were in Lake Charles at that time. I think that was in 1929. It was during the high water, we went to Lake Charles for the high water. It was in 27, I think. Oh, yes, there was a big flood in 27, I remember that. Yeah, in Iberia. Well, we was in Lake Charles, and we stayed over there. And then my mother came up there during the high water. See, I was up there a little before, living with my sister. Is your sister older than you? Yeah, she's older than me. And I quite, I used to go to dances and things. And when Bunk first came to Tony's Bob-Amband in Lake Charles, Louisiana, well, that's where I met him that night. Where was he playing? In Tony's Bob-Amband, in the Lake Charles band. I forgot the other name of it, but I knew it was Tony's Bob-Amband.
Yes. Was one of the called the Eagles, and then there was Ebon Thomas. No, that's not the one.
That's not the one. No, this was a little band in Lake Charles. He had came from, he had just came from Electric, Texas. Electric, Texas.
Yeah. That's where I heard he had been there. I was not even talking to him.

Because he was over there, he said he was working at an undertaker place there. And they wrote for him to come and join this band, and that's where he came there. And so the next day, my brother-in-law brought him over to the house. He asked my brother-in-law who I was. And I told my brother-in-law had knew him, you know, a long time before. So he came on to the house, and he started talking. And then he asked me, would I mind doing him up some shirts? So I told him, yeah. And so he brought the shirts over to my house, and I did up the shirts fine. And then he was living, he had a room, a three-room house right on Pine Street then, because he always did, before living to himself, he said, and not in a rooming house. And he had furniture and everything there. So when I, when I, he came and got the shirts, he thought they were so nicely done. And then from that on he came, kept on coming to see me.
How long did he stay there? Played there quite a while.
Yeah, he played there about a year or two. And then after that.
Did you stay over there and live over there too? Yeah. After the high water too?
Yeah, we lived over there. We came home in 1932. Came back to New Iberia.
New Iberia, 1932, where you married then? Yeah. When did you get married?

Got married when I came back to New Iberia, because we married in New Iberia. In 32? Uh huh. And then we went to, he stayed with this band about a year and a half. Then he went to. Who was the leader again? Tony Bobby. How's that last name?
B-A-B-I-N.
B-A-B-I-N.
Yeah. I didn't know anything about that. Yeah, that's what he just felt.

Yeah, well that's where the band where I met him, where he came to. And he was playing second trumpet then, because this fellow, Harold, I forgot his name, Charlie, Charlie something, I don't know his last name, but he was playing first trumpet.
Do you remember anybody else in that band? Oh no. Anyone like Lawrence Dewey or Clarence?

No, Skinner, I mean I used to play bass. His name was Skinner, that's Nellie Lutcher's daddy. Oh yes. Oh, Lutcher then. Yes, Skinner Lutcher. That's right, I remember hearing that. And Nellie Lutcher was playing piano. She played piano, that's that band the neighborhood, Lutcher's.
Oh yes.
And she played piano. I think, Bunk was playing second.
And Gus, what was his name again? The drummer was, I believe Charlie, I believe Charlie Bowman played drum.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. I forgot who played trombone. It wasn't Gus.
Funny?

Yeah, Funny. No, he was in New Iberia. That was with the band in New Iberia. The Banner Band or something. Yeah. That was the old Banner Band and they called it Colton Roy. Lately they called it Colton Roy.
Is it still going then?

I think it's still going. I don't know. And then after that, he stayed with that band about a year and a half. And he went to Texas on a Labor Day. They went and played in Texas that Labor Day and he didn't come back.
Is that before you were married?

Yeah. And he didn't come back so he sent me over there. And we stayed in Texas about three or four months because I didn't like Texas. And he was going out at night and I was in the house by myself and I was afraid of the stones and things so he decided to come back to Lake Charles. So he came back to Lake Charles but he wasn't playing with nobody then.
He played in Texas though. Yeah. Do you remember who he played with there? Need a chance.
Oh, I forgot the name of the band. Let's see this band man. Which town was that? That was Port Arthur. Port Arthur. Yeah.
There was one piano player, a very good pianist, Lazy Daddy. I think he was in Galveston though. Did you remember ever hearing him? No, I don't remember that.
Phil Moore was his real name.
You all called him Lazy Daddy. No.

I know the man who had sent him for him to play, who he was playing with over there, the man's name was Minor Brown. But I don't know the name of the band because I'm not good on remembering too long. It's different things.
It's hard to remember all those things.
So then when we came back to New Iberia, then after that we got married, then after that he went to, either it was Kansas or Missouri, where we went with a circus. I don't know where it was Kansas.
Well there was one place, Sedalia, Missouri, I know he told me about, he'd been there.
No it wasn't there.

Where he played with the circus band for a while. No it wasn't there. Yeah. The world, I mean the state fair, was there a fair, he was there one year, stopped. But I think he was with the minstrel shows then and just happened to play a little bit with the circus band. Yeah.

Well that's where he had went up there. He might have been in Kansas then too. I think it was in Kansas because I was in New Iberia and then he went up there and he said he was coming back home because he wasn't doing so good up there. And at that time when he was on the way back home he was playing with little short bands in different towns on the way back home. And that's where when he got to Crowley he played a couple of nights with Evanne Thomas' band. When would that be?
About 1932 or 3? About a year after you moved in New Iberia.

Yeah. Then he played, I was surprised that morning when he came on in and that's where he told me that the band. He'd been killed that night and his heart was growing up. Yeah and all the instruments had gone and everything.
Then did he give up his trumpet for a while and stop music?

No he played for a while he had old battle horn he had borrowed from a man named Lee Bowles. That's when he would play with Gus Fontenet and then we couldn't get him a nine thing. And then after that he would, him and his uncle Hendry. Your Bunk's uncle? Yeah.
What was his last name? Johnson's anywhere about it?
No it wasn't Johnson because that wasn't his mother's name. Jefferson, that's the grandmother of Jefferson. I just used to say his uncle Hendry, I forgot his name was Jefferson or what.
I can't remember his mother's name though. Maria Theresa was her first name.
Theresa Johnson. Theresa or something, I thought it was Theresa. Yeah.
But what her name was before Jefferson I guess.
I think it was Jefferson, Theresa Jefferson.
Your grandmother was Jefferson, Rose Jefferson. And so, Uncle Hendry anyway, was that New Iberia too?

Yeah he came in New Iberia at that time. Did he play music? Well there was three of them. Let's see the other ones, they played at little night clubs, you know, nice spots around New Iberia. They had a little, just a trio. And then after that, the Bunk would come home, you know. And that's where he lost his teeth completely one night.
About what time would you say that was, that he lost his teeth and gave up music?
Oh that was in 1934, 35.
35, yeah. It wasn't long after that you see. Yeah. Because you see, he used to, after this accident with Evan Thomas, you see, he used to tie up his plate in his mouth, fix it sometime.
And he used a plate or did he have a bridge or something?

It was a bridge front. It was a bridge front. You see, he had fixed it in there. He used to tie it up or something like that. And I don't know how he lost, completely lost it after that. And then after that he decided that he would go to work in the rice field. So that's where he went to work in the rice field. And then Hall and Kane in the winter time. And he must have worked in the rice field about two or three years.
And over 1939 is when I first worked to him early in 39. Yeah. And he was working there then.
And that's when Louis Armstrong came by.
I think he came by about 1938.
Yeah.
Because I talked to Louis in 38 and he said he'd seen him in New Idea. He said he wasn't playing.

He said he wasn't playing. No, and he wasn't playing then because he didn't have no teeth. And so he had gave it up and he was working at a furniture store at that time. Oh, working at the furniture store. Yeah, he was working at Doatree's furniture store at that time.
Oh, when did he work at Weeks Halls?
Well, he would work off and on at Weeks Hall. He didn't have no study job.
I thought maybe he worked there for a couple of years or something.
No, sometimes the Weeks would call and he'd work there off and on.
Well, I thought he almost stayed there and lived there or something like that. No, he'd go there. No, uh-uh.
And he worked for Frank Doatree even then. And then he was a watchman at night at this place when he was building up the new store. And then after… What store was that? Frank Doatree.
Oh, furniture store.
Well, Big Frank. How's that spelled?
Do you remember? D-A-U-T-R-I-V-E.
Those are French names or Kegian names, whatever they are. I can't get them. Yeah.
D-A-U-T-R-I-V-E. I don't know if you can understand.

And so I think when Louis Armstrong came by, he was in the rice field then. He had quit there and he went to the rice field then. Yeah, I think he must have been there. And after that, well, you started writing to him. Bill Russell started writing to him and everything. That's where he got together and he got his teeth. And then after that, he went and seen the school board. For us. D-Loyd Porter. And he was talking to him about putting up a band, a little school band, teaching school children. So then he had two bands. He had one in Generic, one school band in Generic, and one in New Iberia Elementary School, and one in high school. He had three bands altogether. Then he taught that until 42, I think it was.
Yes, and I still had it in 1942 when Gene Williams came down.
Yeah, I think it was in 42. But in 42 or 43, he went to Frisco.
Yeah, 43, I remember. I have that pretty well lined up in his letters.
Yeah, well, that's when he went to Frisco.

I met him in 1942, so from then on I knew pretty well. But even at that, I didn't know every place he played. Sometime when he'd go back to New Iberia, somebody up in New York or someplace would say they heard that Bunk was playing over in Texas. He played a job or something even over in Texas.
Yeah, he played in Texas. He played in Beaumont, Port Arthur, and all little surrounding places.
In late years was that too, or just in the old days when you first met him?

No, that was just in the old days when I first met him. Somebody told me that? After he got to New Iberia, he didn't go back up there to play. Not for any time. Unless the band, unless he would go out with Gus and them, who would have a date like that or something like that. But he never did go back out there.
Well, I think it would tell me the different places you lived in New Iberia, the address. The first place, do you remember where it was? Well, first place was my own home.
Well, that was 526 Lafayette Street.
That's still the same home?

And the next place we lived was, yeah, that's my first place I lived. The same house that your sisters lived in, yeah. And the next place, well, me and him moved to 5122 School Alley. That's where it was. And that's where it was, were you there in 1938 or 9 when you first, the first letter came to the School Alley? Yeah, that's where we were living.
I remember somebody went over there to take a picture of it once. Yeah, that's where we were living. Somebody said, well, we call this Shirt Tail Alley.
Yeah, that's what they used to call it, then they named it School Alley. Then after that, we moved to 515 Providence.
I never saw that, well, I went by and took a picture of the house once, I believe, but you weren't living there when I went in New Iberia.

And then after that, when the bunk was in Frisco, the man wanted to sell the house, and he couldn't wait until he got back, so I had to find a place. So that's where I moved on 638. They called it Franklin, it was called Franklin Street, but now it's Mylon Street. Oh, yes.
But Lafayette Street is the same.
The same, yeah. So we moved there and we stayed there until he passed away.

I'm wondering a little bit about your life. If you can remember the first music you ever played, I know you played some of the first music you heard when you were a girl. Can you remember any bands around New Iberia? Did you go to hear any dances even from outside or any music in churches? You were Catholic, of course.
Yeah, let's see.
You didn't have any special music like spirituals, I guess, but I mean, I wondered if you ever heard any?

Well, I used to go to Jules Bob Band, used to have a band. They used to come to New Iberia. And of course the Banner Band used to have all the music, because they were most of the standard bands. They'd been there when you were a girl too.
Yeah.

It's an old band. And a lot of them old pieces, what's on the radio, is a lot of them pieces that played in old times. Like, When You're Smiling and all that stuff. Yeah, all those things, they keep on year after year. Yeah.

One thing I was wondering, did they ever have any parades there with the bands, even like for funerals like they have here, or any other kind of parades for the different organizations or lodges that you can remember?
No, they never did have no parades.
There wasn't any brass band, any like the colored brass bands they have here?
No, they never had none of that, yeah. There was nothing like that.
Did they ever bring in a band from New Orleans for a parade of any kind that you ever remember?
No, they never did have no parade. No parades? No.
They had so many here, I thought some of the towns...

Yeah, later they started having the parade, like the Shoebuck. The Sugar Festival now. Oh yes, the Sugar Festival. But that's in the later years they started that. But long ago they never did have none of that.
Did you ever hear any blues singers, that is, were there ever any guitar players and blues singers?

They used to have the Minister's show, used to come, the George Smotset show, used to come there. The Bunk played in that part of the album. But I didn't know him at that time, but he said he played in that. You probably heard him even. Whenever they would come they would have a Minister's show parade, you know. Is that in a tent?
Yeah, in a tent.
Did they have a parade too? Yeah, they'd have a parade that evening, you know, before. Before the show. And then they'd go right to the show. Did you go to some of those?
Did your folks let you go to those?
Yeah, I used to go to the Minister's show. The George Smotset had a good Minister's show. And I forgot all of them.

Did they feature the music very much, do you remember? Yeah. Were there a lot of pieces that aren't, were they all just playing for the songs, or did they play a few pieces themselves as a band or any songs?
No, I didn't ever see, I guess each one was featured. But I never seen much music racks up in them. They had blues singing and things like that, dancing.
Somebody told me Bunk used to put on a little act himself and play a little piece.

Well, you see, I don't remember him so good. But I know one time when we were in Port Arthur, we went to a supermarket. And there was a man they had to remember him in the Minister's show. And I told them about how he used to act and everything in the Minister's show. But I never did know him at that time. No.
You might have missed that year when he put on that act too.
Yeah.
There's a fellow by the name of Weegee Payne. Did you ever know him, the drummer, Weegee? Yeah, I met him.
I met him. I met him in New Iberia. Was he from that part of the country? I don't know where he was from.
He played with Bunk I think in the Banner Band and some of those groups.

So I don't know, I don't forgot where he was from. Let's see, all I know was that this was the old Banner Band, I can call some of them. Oh yeah, that's a funny one. Gestalt Fontenet and Gestalt Fontenet and let's see, where else? So.
Was Lawrence Dewey in the band at any time? Remember it was real light, felt very light. Lawrence Dewey.

And they had William Williams, he was a piano player at that time in some of the old, and he was a drummer, Dennis Adam, he was a drummer and his brother Bird called Adam. And who else it was? At that time William was playing piano before Gus Vaughn and his daughter started playing after that because William died. And I see who else, I can't remember. See, sometimes I have to see those people. I'm the same right now. Can't think of the names of the band. Because that's the story, I ain't good on, I can't remember, you know, that, but I can't remember names so well, that's one thing I can't do, unless I see a person. Do you think there are any pictures much of that band?

I saw one picture from a poster, it wasn't very clear, that Lawrence Dewey, the clarinetist had. The Banner Band? With Bunk and it also had Yvonne Thomas in it. Yeah. They called it the, does Yvonne play there too?
Yeah, he used to play in it, uh-huh. He used to play in it, uh-huh. In the dinner too. Well, see they used to go and come, you know. Yeah, he used to play in it.

Do you know anybody, did you ever see any good photographs of that, anybody that might have pictures of it over there? No, I don't know if I have a picture of it. We'll try to talk to Gus sometime, we'll have an interview with him sometime when we get over there.
Yeah, because he can tell you more about it. Maybe he can keep going, I guess. Yeah, uh-huh.
Do you know where he lives by the way, or how we could locate him? Who, Gus, aren't there?

He lives across the by, I forgot the name of the street, but I know where you are. We're on the north side of the side. Yeah, uh-huh. Well, he waits for the plan was now, and he always got this ball on, so. You get there, you can find him. I forgot the name of the street where he lives on, but it's across the by. Works for the, uh, who does he work for?
That's he, the planter.
He have a liquor store and bar room and everything.
Yeah, the planter, the planter, LA, LA. We can look that up in the phone book or someplace out there. Yeah. Find it too.

Uh-huh. Now you get to know, I better just call my sister, she can give her the name of the street. Oh, she know, sure. Yeah, she know where he lives. I know where he lives, but I can't know where he's at.

I might even have his address in my old notes, but I used to try to find him. Uh-huh. I used to take notes when I'd go to visit you about and talk to Bunk sometime, but I don't know where I'd find him, right, in a hurry. To return back to your life, did you ever take up any instrument when you were young and learn any? No.
Uh-huh. Yeah, when I was in school I went to music lessons or piano. Uh-huh. And that's about three or four months then after I stopped. Uh-huh. Her name was Mrs. Florence Pemberton. Uh-huh.
Did you learn to play pretty well or did you give it up before you?
I learned enough to know the notes and read a little bit. Yeah. So that's why I can help Bunk a little bit on his notes and things. Uh-huh.
Did you want to learn an instrument always or when you were young did you want to be a musician? No, I used to try to go on Bunk's trumpet sometime and used to try to teach him.
Did he teach you a little bit then? Yeah.

Some other day I want to talk to you about that too. What he tried to teach you and how he taught you. Oh, sometimes we couldn't get along without putting the thing down. Was there any other instrument that you ever tried to teach the trumpet? No, that's all. How long did you work on that trumpet or blow on it all together?
Oh, it was about two or three months. I guess in all, you know, not study but now I know. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no.
No, no. No, no. No, no.
No, no.
No, no. No, no. No, no. No, no.
No, no. No, no. You never got that? No, no, no. You never got that? No, no.
You never got that?
No, no.
You never got that? No, you never got that far.

But I know enough, you know, to show Bunky, you know, was there about it. Because I used to watch him, you know, what he'd do on his. So that's why I can teach Bunky, about keeping his and clean and everything, you know. So.
You see, can you think of any other jobs Bunky had in those years that you knew? Any other bands?
Well, that's all the bands that he played in.
You see, there's one called the Black Eagle, I believe.
Oh, that was before my time.
That was the, I thought that was the Yvonne Thomas band, though. Well, that was late.

That was, you see, they had the Black Eagle was a band long before that, you see. And he and Thomas just got up this band, you see, and. Just used that name again. Yeah, uh-huh. But the Black Eagle band was old.
But the Banner band was the main one in that section.
Yeah, it was the main one. The Black Eagle band was mostly from Crowley. Yeah, because it wasn't the Iberia band.
Oh, it was mostly Crowley.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Were there any other bands in any other towns around, like Lafayette or St. Charles? No. That you can remember?
They never had no band in Lafayette at all, because the Banner band thing used to always go over there.
About how often did they have good bands coming to New Iberia for dances? That is like-
Well, in my time, every 15 they would have a band, you know. The 15th? The 15th, yes. Every month? Yeah, every 15th day they would have a big band. Every 15th day. At that time.
Oh, it was twice a month then?
Yeah, uh-huh.
I wonder, did there many big bands like Armstrong or Ellington or those things come?

Well, just in the later years, those big bands started coming in. Come through there? Yeah, but most of the time they used little bands out on the wall, like Papa Celestine used to come in. Come out of New Iberia. Yeah, he used to come in and play in. New Barbering band. He was from New, somewhere around here. They used to come out there. But this later years, a big band started going out there.

Was there much, of course, I know you didn't get around to all the bar rooms, but I mean, do you think there were many bands working there, like on Saturday nights every week in some of the small places, maybe two or three musicians? Did Bunk ever work any little jobs like that, Justin?

Well, that's what, yeah, that's what I told him and his Uncle Henry used to work little jobs like that. And Bird Guard Adams as well. And this was, I think it was just four of them. I can't remember, the other one's name was Minor. I don't know, I forgot his name. But he died. But he was playing banjo. And they used to work little jobs like that on Saturday night at a, let me see what this was, a place of man was. They used to work there every Saturday night, this man named, I forgot his name. He had a place of business. And they used to go there and play.

I was always going to talk to Weeks Hall some more because he acted like he knew Bunk very well. Yeah. He did. I guess he did. But like, somebody told me they used to put on parties there at his house and he'd have
a band here and just Bunk together. He used to have them come up there and play. Because he used to have big parties at that time.
Oh, well I think of it, who was that family that you all worked for, that, uh,
the Russian?
The one in real... The Barmystrow. Yeah.
The Russian and the Barmystrow had a shirt plantation in Cuba or something. Uh-huh.
How's that name spelled again, do you know?
Uh, B-R-O-N-S-T-R-O-W, I believe, I forgot. How do you say it again?
Barmystrow. Uh, I have a picture of that old house. It was a nice house.

That was the Della Luce old house. Is that right on that main street or is it back a block from, uh... It's right across from Weeks Hall, about three or four houses. Towards New Iberia. I mean towards New Orleans. Yeah, right on Main Street. Main Street. Uh-huh. And, uh, Bunk used to work for them when I was working there. He worked there a while. Uh-huh.
That was in pretty late years, wasn't it?
Yeah, that's in the late years. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Well, when he worked in the rice fields, what did he do? Did he actually do field work? Like cutting the rice or whatever they call it? Yeah.

Or just haul it? Uh-huh. No, he was driving tractors. Driving tractors, yeah. In the rice field. You know, they was hauling the rice. Yeah. And then they hauled the rice from the field to the mill. Uh-huh. And then after that, when that would be over, then he would go and haul cane. It would be cane season then.
Uh-huh. Now what is the rice season? Is that in the summer?
Yeah, it's around in August. August. Yeah.
The cane season comes in the winter about when that canes.
Right, in the last of September. Last of September. Uh-huh.
And they worked hauling the cane. Yeah. I'm trying to think if there's anything else about your life in particular that you'd want to say about your musical experiences.
That's all the musical experience that I had.
Did you go to many dances? I'm not trying to get personal and all that, but I just want to mention.

Oh, when I was in Lake Charles, I didn't used to miss a dance. You didn't miss something in your life, though. No. But that's where I probably met him at a dance in West Hall. This hall was on, what street now? Franklin, not Franklin Street. I could go to the prison. It's been so long. I can't remember all the things. Tell me this.
Did Bunk ever dance with you? He never did dance.

He never did dance. I didn't think so. He always said that he played music for you to dance, but he wouldn't dance. He wouldn't, you never saw him out on the floor to dance. But the only thing he would dance if he'd get high and he'd be in a ballroom or something in a jukebox or something like that. Oh yeah, a jukebox or something like that. He'd get there and dance. But otherwise, like men would come down and get somebody their seat. He never did do that. He wouldn't come down and dance with you?
No. No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No.
No. No. No. No. No. No.
Just about five years he was out of a horn.
Did he seem to be unhappy when he couldn't play music without it or was he just resigned to it? Or did he seem to mind it much that he didn't play anymore and miss it a lot?
Well, I think he didn't miss it. Cause he used to, cause then after that, before he got a horn, he was playing a bass horn, one of the school's bass horn with Gus Fontaine.
He would be on bass. Before he had his false teeth or even or not? Did he do anything at all when he?

No, he didn't. No, that was after he had got his false teeth. I forgot about that too. Yeah, he was playing with Donald Marsh, Rufus Smith, and Gus Fontaine and Mercedes, I forgot what Harold's last name is. And the boy who played trumpet was named Harold, I forgot his last name, but his wife was playing piano.
Did he borrow that horn or wasn't his?
No, it was one of the school bass horns he would take. Oh, I see, yeah. Yeah, and he'd play bass on until he got a good trumpet. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Did he ever play anything else that you knew? Once in Texas he said he played saxophone. Did you ever know him when he played saxophone?
Well, once he was in Texas he had an old clarinet. Like, you know, he would double up on that. Double up on that.
Was that when you were married or before that time? That was before. Before that time.
Mm-hmm. That's when we were in Texas. Over there.
Yeah. Is there anything else about your family that you can think of? Any other musicians in your family? Your father play anything?
No, my father was a carpenter. He was a carpenter. Yeah. I forgot to ask that.
Well, we're just about out of tape here now. Yeah. So I guess that's about all the questions we can get in. I'll let that one do it. Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Opening and Maude Johnson's birth in New Iberia
segments.summary: Maude Bakke Johnson states her name, birth date (1908) and birthplace, New Iberia, Louisiana.

segments.title: Bakke family, relatives and her sister's husband Candy Dixon
segments.summary: She spells her father's name, discusses relation to clarinetist George Bakke, her dead brothers and her sister in New Iberia whose husband Candy knew Bunk.

segments.title: Meeting Bunk in Lake Charles at Tony Babin's band
segments.summary: During the high water she lived in Lake Charles, met Bunk at a dance when he joined the band from Electra, Texas; he had her launder his shirts and began visiting. They returned to New Iberia in 1932.

segments.title: Marriage and the Lake Charles band's members
segments.summary: They married in New Iberia in 1932. She recalls Bunk as second trumpet in Babin's band, with Skinner Lutcher on bass and Nellie Lutcher on piano.

segments.title: Banner Band and Bunk's trip to Texas
segments.summary: After a mostly muttered stretch, she recalls the Banner Band and that Bunk left on Labor Day for Texas; she followed but disliked Texas and they returned to Lake Charles.

segments.title: Bunk's Texas bands and Lazy Daddy
segments.summary: Discussion of who Bunk played with in Port Arthur, Lazy Daddy (Phil Moore) and Minor Brown; she cannot recall the band name.

segments.title: Circus and minstrel work, and Evan Thomas's band in Crowley
segments.summary: Bunk went north with a circus or minstrel show, and on the way home played with Evan Thomas's band in Crowley, the night the band was in a disaster.

segments.title: Borrowed horn, Gus Fontenette and Uncle Hendry's trio
segments.summary: Bunk played a borrowed horn with Gus Fontenette and then in a trio with his uncle Hendry; the family name Jefferson is discussed.

segments.title: Losing his teeth, rice field work and Louis Armstrong's visit
segments.summary: Bunk lost his bridge around 1934-35, quit music for rice field and furniture store work; Armstrong came by around 1938 when he was not playing.

segments.title: Weeks Hall and Frank Doatree's furniture store jobs
segments.summary: Bunk worked off and on for Weeks Hall and for Frank Doatree's furniture store, where he was also night watchman.

segments.title: New teeth, school bands and leaving for San Francisco
segments.summary: With Bill Russell's help Bunk got teeth, taught three school bands until about 1942, then went to San Francisco in 1942-43; his Texas playing was in the old days.

segments.title: Houses where they lived in New Iberia
segments.summary: She lists their addresses in New Iberia, from Lafayette Street through School Alley and Providence Street to Franklin Street, where they stayed until Bunk died.

segments.title: Music in New Iberia: Banner Band and absence of parades
segments.summary: She recalls hearing the Banner Band and old standards, and says New Iberia had no parades or brass bands until the later Sugar Festival.

segments.title: Minstrel shows and blues singing
segments.summary: The George Smart minstrel show came with tent parades, blues singing and dancing; Bunk played in them before she knew him.

segments.title: Banner Band members and locating Gus Fontenette
segments.summary: She names Banner Band members including Weegee Payne, William Williams and the Adam brothers, and they discuss where Gus lives for a future interview.

segments.title: Her piano lessons and trying Bunk's trumpet
segments.summary: She took piano lessons briefly with Mrs. Florence Pemberton, tried Bunk's trumpet for a few months, and helped him with notes and horn care.

segments.chapter: Local bands and Bunk's later jobs
segments.title: Black Eagle band, dance bands in the area and Bunk's Saturday jobs
segments.summary: The Black Eagle band was from Crowley, the Banner Band was main locally; bands played every 15th, and Bunk worked small Saturday jobs with Uncle Henry and Bird Adams. Weeks Hall hosted parties.

segments.chapter: Local bands and Bunk's later jobs
segments.title: Working for the Bronstrow family and rice and cane field work
segments.summary: Bunk worked for the Bronstrow family near Weeks Hall late on, and drove tractors hauling rice and then cane.

segments.title: Dances and Bunk not dancing
segments.summary: She never missed a dance in Lake Charles; Bunk played for dancers but would not dance himself except when drunk.

segments.title: Five years without a horn, school bass horn and clarinet
segments.summary: She thinks he did not miss playing; after getting teeth he played a school bass horn with Gus Fontenette's group, and had doubled on clarinet in Texas.

segments.title: Her father and closing of the tape
segments.summary: Her father was a carpenter, not a musician; the tape ends.
